questions.q: What mode of delivery is generally preferred in eclampsia after stabilization?
opts: Operative vaginal delivery for every case
questions.exp: The source lists vaginal delivery as the usual mode; cesarean is for an obstetric indication. (Book p402)

questions.q: When is cesarean section indicated in eclampsia according to the notes?
opts: In every woman with a seizure
questions.exp: Cesarean section is indicated only for an obstetric indication. (Book p402)

questions.q: Which anesthetic approach is written for eclampsia delivery on this page?
opts: Spinal anesthesia is mandatory in every case
questions.exp: The p402 eclampsia delivery note lists general anesthesia. (Book p402)

questions.q: In which pre-eclampsia population is impending eclampsia seen?
opts: Mild PE without severe features only
questions.exp: Impending eclampsia is seen in patients with severe pre-eclampsia. (Book p402)

questions.q: What is the most common warning symptom of impending eclampsia listed, with its approximate frequency?
questions.exp: Severe headache is the most common stated symptom, occurring in about 70%. (Book p402)

questions.q: What is the suggested cause of epigastric pain in impending eclampsia?
questions.exp: Epigastric pain is attributed to a subcapsular hematoma. (Book p402)

questions.q: What is the correct sequence of management for impending eclampsia?
opts: Magnesium sulfate, antihypertensives, then termination after stabilization
Immediate discharge, then aspirin at 36 weeks
Salt restriction, then bed rest only
questions.exp: MgSO4 prevents seizures, antihypertensives treat BP, and pregnancy is terminated after stabilization regardless of gestation. (Book p402)

questions.q: A 24-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks has an eclamptic convulsion. She is stabilised with magnesium sulfate and her blood pressure is controlled. When should the baby be delivered?
opts: Once the mother is stabilised, usually within 24 hours, regardless of gestation
By immediate caesarean section within thirty minutes of the fit
After waiting two weeks so antenatal corticosteroids can be given
At 37 weeks, because eclampsia alone never justifies preterm delivery
questions.exp: Eclampsia is an indication for delivery once the mother is stabilised and seizures are controlled; only maternal stabilisation is delayed, not delivery itself. (Book p402)

questions.q: Which visual change is recognized as a pre-eclampsia visual disturbance?
questions.exp: Blurred vision, scotoma, diplopia, and blindness are listed visual disturbances. (Book p402)

questions.q: How common is blindness in severe pre-eclampsia according to the notes?
questions.exp: Blindness is listed in 10–15% of severe pre-eclampsia cases. (Book p402)

questions.q: What is the usual prognosis of blindness associated with severe pre-eclampsia?
questions.exp: Blindness in severe PE is usually reversible. (Book p402)

questions.q: Which condition is an exception that can make PE-associated blindness irreversible?
opts: Retinal artery occlusion or retinal detachment
A mild headache relieved by medication
questions.exp: Retinal-artery occlusion or retinal detachment are listed exceptions to reversibility. (Book p402)

questions.q: Which cause of visual loss is also called amaurosis fugax in the notes?
questions.exp: Occipital blindness is labelled amaurosis fugax. (Book p402)

questions.q: Which retinal cause of visual loss is termed Purtscher retinopathy?
questions.exp: Retinal infarction is termed Purtscher retinopathy in the notes. (Book p402)

questions.q: Which classification is used for hypertensive retinopathy?
questions.exp: Hypertensive retinopathy is classified by Keith–Wagener classification. (Book p402)

questions.sec: Visual symptoms in PE & hypertensive retinopathy
questions.q: Match the visual problem with its basis — 1) Blurring and scotomata 2) Cortical blindness with a normal eye examination 3) Retinal arteriolar narrowing on fundoscopy … A) Occipital vasogenic oedema of posterior reversible encephalopathy B) Warning symptom of impending eclampsia from retinal and cerebral vasospasm C) Generalised vasospasm of the retinal arterioles in severe pre-eclampsia
questions.exp: Visual symptoms warn of impending eclampsia, cortical blindness points to PRES, and fundoscopy shows arteriolar spasm with haemorrhages or papilloedema. (Book p402)

questions.q: After an eclamptic seizure, what should be checked first in the fetal-distress algorithm?
questions.exp: The stepwise algorithm first checks fetal heart sound. (Book p402)

questions.q: If fetal distress persists after an eclamptic seizure, what must be ruled out before/with cesarean consideration?
questions.exp: With persistent fetal distress, the source directs clinicians to rule out abruptio placentae and consider cesarean. (Book p402)

questions.q: If fetal heart sound becomes normal after an eclamptic seizure, what is the next step?
opts: Perform immediate cesarean solely for the prior tracing
questions.exp: Normalization of FHS directs continuation of eclampsia management. (Book p402)

questions.q: Fill up: During and immediately after an eclamptic convulsion the fetal heart rate usually shows ______, which recovers within ______.
opts: a persistent tachycardia; about an hour
no change at all; it needs no observation
questions.exp: Fetal bradycardia during a fit is common and usually recovers within minutes as maternal oxygenation and uterine blood flow improve. (Book p402)

questions.q: What persistent BP threshold is cited from NICE for starting antihypertensive therapy in PIH?
opts: At least 140/90 mmHg after one reading only
questions.exp: The source cites NICE treatment for persistent BP ≥150/100 mmHg. (Book p403)

questions.q: What systolic target range is stated while treating hypertension in pregnancy?
questions.exp: The stated systolic treatment target is 130–140 mmHg. (Book p403)

questions.q: What diastolic target range is stated while treating hypertension in pregnancy?
questions.exp: The stated diastolic treatment target is 80–90 mmHg. (Book p403)

questions.q: Why should BP not be overcorrected in pregnancy?
opts: It can reduce uteroplacental perfusion and cause fetal distress
questions.exp: Overcorrection can lower uteroplacental perfusion and precipitate fetal distress. (Book p403)

questions.q: Which trio is listed as first-line antihypertensive drugs for pre-eclampsia?
questions.exp: Labetalol, hydralazine, and nifedipine are the first-line drugs. (Book p403)

questions.q: Which drug is listed as least preferred among other antihypertensive options?
questions.exp: Nitroprusside is noted as least preferred. (Book p403)

questions.q: What BP threshold defines severe PE/hypertensive crisis requiring IV antihypertensive therapy?
questions.exp: BP ≥160/110 mmHg is treated as hypertensive crisis with IV antihypertensives. (Book p403)

questions.q: Fill up: Antihypertensive drug treatment is started when the blood pressure is persistently above ______ mmHg, and a hypertensive crisis is a pressure above ______ mmHg.
questions.exp: Treatment thresholds aim to prevent cerebral haemorrhage: sustained pressures above 150/100 are treated and above 160/110 are a crisis needing urgent control. (Book p403)

questions.q: What is the first IV labetalol dose in the severe-PE sequence?
questions.exp: The IV labetalol sequence starts with 20 mg. (Book p403)

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes escalation of IV labetalol in the notes?
opts: 20 mg, then 40 mg, then 80 mg, then 80 mg at 15-minute checks
questions.exp: The stated labetalol escalation is 20→40→80→80 mg, checking BP every 15 minutes. (Book p403)

questions.q: What is the maximum IV labetalol dose in the source algorithm?
questions.exp: The maximum labetalol dose is 220 mg. (Book p403)

questions.q: In whom is labetalol contraindicated according to the notes?
opts: A patient with fetal growth restriction
A patient with bradycardia or asthma
questions.exp: Labetalol is contraindicated in bradycardia and asthma. (Book p403)

questions.q: What is the IV hydralazine sequence for hypertensive crisis?
opts: 5 mg IV, then 10 mg IV after 20 minutes if needed
questions.exp: Hydralazine is 5 mg IV followed by 10 mg IV after 20 minutes if required. (Book p403)

questions.q: What is the maximum hydralazine dose in the source algorithm?
questions.exp: The maximum hydralazine dose is 30 mg. (Book p403)

questions.q: How should nifedipine be given for severe PIH according to the notes?
opts: It is contraindicated in all PE
questions.exp: The source explicitly states oral nifedipine, not sublingual nifedipine. (Book p403)

questions.q: Match the antihypertensive with its description — 1) Labetalol 2) Nifedipine 3) Hydralazine … A) Calcium channel blocker given orally, useful where there is no intravenous access B) Combined alpha and beta blocker given intravenously in escalating boluses C) Direct arteriolar vasodilator given intravenously, with more hypotension than the others
questions.exp: Labetalol is the intravenous workhorse, oral or short-acting nifedipine is an alternative, and hydralazine causes more maternal hypotension. (Book p403)

questions.q: Which oral drugs are first-line options for chronic hypertension in pregnancy?
questions.exp: Methyldopa, labetalol, and nifedipine are listed oral first-line drugs for chronic HTN. (Book p403)

questions.q: Why is alpha-methyldopa not used as first-line therapy for severe PE?
questions.exp: Alpha-methyldopa is slow acting and therefore not first line for severe PE. (Book p403)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about diuretics in pre-eclampsia is TRUE?
opts: Diuretics are avoided, because the plasma volume is already contracted and perfusion of the placenta would fall further
Frusemide is the first-line drug for the acute control of severe hypertension in pregnancy
Thiazide diuretics are given routinely to all pregnant women to prevent pre-eclampsia
Frusemide is used routinely in severe pre-eclampsia to protect renal function
questions.exp: Pre-eclampsia is a state of vasospasm with a contracted intravascular volume, so diuretics worsen perfusion; they are reserved for pulmonary oedema. (Book p403)

questions.q: Which medication class is contraindicated as an antihypertensive in pregnancy?
questions.exp: ACE inhibitors are listed as contraindicated in pregnancy. (Book p404)

questions.q: Which antihypertensive receptor-blocking class, exemplified by losartan, is contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.exp: ARBs such as losartan are contraindicated. (Book p404)

questions.q: Which beta-blocker statement is correct in pregnancy according to the source?
opts: All beta-blockers including labetalol are mandatory
questions.exp: The notes list beta-blockers as contraindicated with the exception of labetalol. (Book p404)

questions.q: Why are diuretics contraindicated in pre-eclampsia?
questions.exp: Diuretics are contraindicated in PE because of hemoconcentration. (Book p404)

questions.q: In which setting can a diuretic be used despite its contraindication in PE?
opts: Pulmonary edema or congestive heart failure
questions.exp: Diuretics may be used for pulmonary edema and congestive heart failure; in chronic HTN they are not first line and should be used before 20 weeks. (Book p404)

questions.q: What is the primary use of magnesium sulfate in a hypertensive pregnant woman?
opts: Induction of labor in all pregnancies
questions.exp: MgSO4 is used for prevention and treatment of seizures in hypertensive pregnancy. (Book p404)

questions.q: How is magnesium sulfate described pharmacologically in the notes?
opts: A centrally acting drug acting on NMDA receptors
questions.exp: MgSO4 is centrally acting and acts on NMDA receptors. (Book p404)

questions.q: Which effect of MgSO4 helps protect the brain in eclampsia?
opts: Loss of the neuronal membrane potential in the cerebral cortex
Reduced cerebral edema and oxidative stress, with membrane stabilisation
Increased cerebral edema, which lowers the seizure threshold
Increased free-radical production within the cerebral cortex
questions.exp: MgSO4 protects the brain in eclampsia by reducing cerebral edema and oxidative stress and by stabilising membranes. (Book p404)

questions.q: What therapeutic range is stated for magnesium sulfate in the source notes?
questions.exp: The notes state a narrow therapeutic range of 4–7 mg. (Book p404)

questions.q: Which MgSO4 regimen is followed in India according to the notes?
questions.exp: The Pritchard regimen is stated as followed in India. (Book p404)

questions.q: What IM component is given in the Pritchard loading dose?
opts: 10 g of 50% MgSO4, 5 g in each buttock
4 g of 20% MgSO4 in each buttock
questions.exp: Pritchard loading includes 10 g 50% MgSO4 IM, divided as 5 g per buttock. (Book p404)

questions.q: What IV component is given in the Pritchard loading dose?
questions.exp: The Pritchard loading dose also includes 4 g of 20% MgSO4 IV. (Book p404)

questions.q: Fill up: Magnesium sulfate prevents eclamptic seizures by antagonising ______ at the neuromuscular junction and by blocking ______ receptors in the brain.
questions.exp: Magnesium is a physiological calcium antagonist and blocks NMDA glutamate receptors, which is why it prevents and treats eclamptic seizures. (Book p404)

questions.q: In the source preparation note, one 2-mL ampoule of 50% MgSO4 contains how much MgSO4?
questions.exp: One 2-mL ampoule of 50% MgSO4 contains 1 g. (Book p404)

questions.q: How many 2-mL 50% MgSO4 ampoules are needed for the 10-g IM loading component?
questions.exp: Ten 1-g ampoules are required for the 10-g IM loading dose. (Book p404)

questions.q: How is the 4-g IV Pritchard loading dose prepared in the source notes?
opts: Four ampoules plus 12 mL normal saline to make 20 mL of about 20% solution
Four ampoules in 500 mL Ringer lactate
questions.exp: Four ampoules with 12 mL NS make 20 mL containing 4 g, approximately 20% MgSO4. (Book p404)

questions.q: Fill up: In the Pritchard regimen the maintenance dose is ______ g of magnesium sulfate intramuscularly every ______ hours, continued for 24 hours after delivery.
questions.exp: After the 4 g intravenous and 10 g intramuscular loading dose, 5 g is given intramuscularly every 4 hours, usually for 24 hours after delivery. (Book p404)

questions.q: Is renal function checked before the Pritchard loading dose according to the notes?
opts: No; loading is given irrespective of renal status
Yes; a normal creatinine is required
questions.exp: The notes state renal function is not checked before loading; loading is given irrespective of renal status. (Book p405)

questions.q: What maternal parameter should be monitored while giving IV MgSO4?
questions.exp: Maternal heart rate is monitored during IV administration. (Book p405)

questions.q: What is the Pritchard IM maintenance dose and schedule?
opts: 5 g of 50% solution IM every 4 hours in alternate buttocks
10 g IM once daily in the same buttock
questions.exp: Maintenance is 5 g of 50% MgSO4 IM every 4 hours in alternate buttocks. (Book p405)

questions.q: How long is Pritchard maintenance continued?
opts: Only until the seizure stops, after which the magnesium is discontinued
For seven days after delivery, to cover the late risk of seizures
Until 20 weeks of gestation in cases of early severe disease
Until 24 hours after delivery or 24 hours after the last convulsion, whichever is later
questions.exp: Maintenance continues for 24 hours after delivery or 24 hours after the last convulsion, whichever comes later. (Book p405)

questions.q: Which deep-tendon-reflex finding is required before each MgSO4 maintenance dose?
questions.exp: A present knee jerk/deep tendon reflex is required before maintenance. (Book p405)

questions.q: What minimum respiratory rate is required before MgSO4 maintenance?
questions.exp: Respiratory rate must be at least 12/min. (Book p405)

questions.q: What minimum urine output is required before MgSO4 maintenance?
questions.exp: Urine output must be at least 100 cc over 4 hours. (Book p405)

questions.q: Which MgSO4 regimen is recommended by ACOG in the notes?
questions.exp: The notes identify Zuspan/Sibai as ACOG recommended. (Book p405)

questions.q: What is the IV loading dose in the Zuspan/Sibai regimen?
opts: 4–6 g in 100 mL IV fluid over 15–20 minutes
questions.exp: Zuspan/Sibai loading is 4–6 g in 100 mL IV fluid over 15–20 minutes. (Book p405)

questions.q: What is the IV maintenance infusion rate in the Zuspan/Sibai regimen?
questions.exp: Zuspan/Sibai maintenance is 1–2 g/hour in IV infusion. (Book p405)

questions.q: What is the first clinical sign of magnesium sulfate toxicity?
questions.exp: Loss of the knee jerk is the first toxicity sign. (Book p405)

questions.q: At approximately what serum magnesium level is loss of knee jerk expected?
questions.exp: Loss of knee jerk occurs at about 9–10 mEq/L. (Book p405)

questions.q: What toxicity occurs at about 12 mEq/L of magnesium?
opts: Respiratory depression progressing to respiratory arrest
Loss of the knee jerk with reflexes otherwise preserved
Cardiac arrhythmia with a normal respiratory rate
Normal deep tendon reflexes with no change in respiration
questions.exp: At about 12 mEq/L of magnesium, respiratory depression and then respiratory arrest occur. (Book p405)

questions.q: What toxicity occurs at about 15 mEq/L of magnesium?
questions.exp: Cardiac arrhythmia occurs at about 15 mEq/L. (Book p405)

questions.q: A woman receiving magnesium sulfate for severe pre-eclampsia has a respiratory rate of 10/min, absent knee jerks and a urine output of 20 mL per hour. What is the immediate management?
opts: Stop the magnesium infusion, give 1 g of calcium gluconate intravenously and support ventilation
Continue magnesium at half the maintenance dose and review in four hours
Give frusemide to raise the urine output and continue magnesium as before
Give neostigmine to reverse the neuromuscular blockade and continue magnesium
questions.exp: Loss of reflexes, respiratory depression and oliguria are magnesium toxicity, reversed by stopping the infusion and giving intravenous calcium gluconate. (Book p405)

questions.q: At what magnesium level is cardiac arrest listed?
questions.exp: Cardiac arrest is listed at about 24 mEq/L. (Book p405)

questions.q: Is oliguria itself a sign of magnesium sulfate toxicity?
opts: Yes, oliguria is the very first sign of magnesium toxicity
Yes, oliguria proves that cardiac arrest is imminent
No, oliguria has no relevance at all to magnesium dosing
No; it prompts monitoring because MgSO4 is renally excreted
questions.exp: Oliguria is not itself a sign of magnesium sulfate toxicity; it prompts monitoring because MgSO4 is excreted by the kidney. (Book p405)

questions.q: What is the antidote for magnesium sulfate toxicity?
questions.exp: The antidote is 10 mL 10% calcium gluconate intravenously. (Book p405)

questions.q: Which set of conditions receives MgSO4 for seizure prevention in the notes?
opts: Severe PE, impending PE, and HELLP syndrome
Mild PE only, with no severe features
questions.exp: MgSO4 prevents seizures in severe PE, impending PE, and HELLP syndrome; it treats eclamptic seizures. (Book p405)

questions.q: For which preterm-labor gestational age is MgSO4 used for fetal neuroprotection?
questions.exp: The source lists neuroprotection in preterm labor before 32 weeks. (Book p405)

questions.q: What is the note on tocolytic use of MgSO4?
opts: It is the universal first-line tocolytic at any dose
It is used only to cause seizures
It is dose dependent and not used for this because seizure occurs at tocolytic concentrations
questions.exp: Tocolysis is dose-dependent; the source says MgSO4 is not used because seizure appears at the tocolytic concentration. (Book p405)

questions.q: All of the following are accepted uses of magnesium sulfate in obstetrics EXCEPT:
opts: Augmentation of slow progress in the first stage of labour
Fetal neuroprotection before very preterm birth
Short-term tocolysis to allow transfer or corticosteroids
questions.exp: Magnesium is not a uterotonic: it relaxes myometrium, so it is used for tocolysis, neuroprotection and eclampsia, never for augmentation. (Book p405)

questions.q: What does HELLP stand for?
opts: Hypertension, edema, liver pain, low protein
Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelet count
questions.exp: HELLP means hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count. (Book p406)

questions.q: How many HELLP components must be present for diagnosis according to the notes?
questions.exp: All three components must be present for HELLP diagnosis. (Book p406)

questions.q: HELLP syndrome is primarily a complication of which disorder?
questions.exp: HELLP is a complication of severe PE, with more severe hepatic involvement and hemolysis. (Book p406)

questions.q: In what proportion of HELLP cases is BP raised according to the notes?
questions.exp: Raised BP is present in about 80–85% of HELLP cases. (Book p406)

questions.q: In which parity group is HELLP more common?
questions.exp: The source states HELLP is more common in multigravida women. (Book p406)

questions.q: When does HELLP commonly present?
opts: Third trimester, and it may appear within 48 hours after delivery
Only before 12 weeks of gestation in early pregnancy
Only after 12 weeks following delivery in the puerperium
Only during labour presenting before 20 weeks of gestation
questions.exp: HELLP commonly presents in the third trimester, and it may also be seen within 48 hours after delivery. (Book p406)

questions.q: What is the most common symptom of HELLP syndrome in the notes?
questions.exp: Right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain is the most common listed symptom, followed by jaundice. (Book p406)

questions.q: Fill up: The acronym HELLP stands for ______.
opts: Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets
Hypertension, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets
Haemolysis, elevated lactate and low platelets
Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low protein
questions.exp: HELLP is haemolysis with schistocytes, raised transaminases and thrombocytopenia, a severe variant of pre-eclampsia. (Book p406)

questions.q: Which peripheral-smear finding supports hemolysis in Tennessee HELLP criteria?
questions.exp: Burr cells or schistocytes on peripheral smear support hemolysis. (Book p406)

questions.q: Which bilirubin level supports hemolysis in Tennessee HELLP criteria?
questions.exp: Serum bilirubin ≥1.2 mg/dL is one hemolysis marker. (Book p406)

questions.q: Which LDH value supports hemolysis in Tennessee HELLP criteria?
questions.exp: LDH ≥600 IU/mL supports hemolysis in Tennessee criteria. (Book p406)

questions.q: What serum haptoglobin level supports hemolysis in Tennessee HELLP criteria?
questions.exp: Low haptoglobin, below 25 mg/dL, is a hemolysis marker. (Book p406)

questions.q: What liver-enzyme threshold supports the “EL” component of HELLP?
questions.exp: Elevated SGOT/SGPT at least two times normal fulfills the liver-enzyme component. (Book p406)

questions.q: Why is alkaline phosphatase not used in HELLP diagnosis?
opts: It is always zero in pregnancy
It is not a liver enzyme
questions.exp: ALP is normally increased in pregnancy, so it is not used for HELLP diagnosis. (Book p406)

questions.q: What platelet count fulfills the low-platelet component of HELLP?
questions.exp: Low platelet count is below 1 lakh/mm³. (Book p406)

questions.q: Match the term with its meaning — 1) Complete or class 1 HELLP 2) Partial HELLP 3) Mississippi classification … A) Platelets below 50,000 with AST above 70 IU/L and LDH above 600 IU/L B) Only one or two of the three components are present C) Classes 1 to 3 are defined by the lowest recorded platelet count
questions.exp: Tennessee criteria define complete HELLP numerically, partial HELLP has incomplete features, and Mississippi grades severity purely by platelet nadir. (Book p406)

questions.q: What immediate stabilization medications are used in HELLP before definitive treatment?
questions.exp: Initial HELLP management includes MgSO4 for seizure prevention and antihypertensives. (Book p406)

questions.q: What is the definitive treatment for HELLP syndrome?
opts: Observation until 40 weeks in all cases
questions.exp: Definitive treatment is delivery/termination irrespective of gestational age. (Book p406)

questions.q: What is the delivery instruction after the first corticosteroid dose in HELLP?
questions.exp: The page specifies first corticosteroid dose followed by immediate induction of labor. (Book p406)

questions.q: A 30-year-old at 31 weeks has HELLP syndrome with platelets of 85,000, AST of 120 IU/L, epigastric tenderness and a blood pressure of 150/100 mmHg. What is the management?
opts: Stabilise her, give corticosteroids, and deliver once she is stable, usually within 24-48 hours
Immediate caesarean section without waiting for corticosteroids
Expectant management until 37 weeks because the platelet count is still above 50,000
Therapeutic plasma exchange as first-line treatment before considering delivery
questions.exp: HELLP is an indication for delivery after maternal stabilisation and steroids; plasma exchange is reserved for refractory postpartum disease. (Book p406)

questions.q: What is listed as a differential diagnosis for HELLP syndrome?
questions.exp: AFLP is listed as a differential diagnosis for HELLP. (Book p407)

questions.q: Which obstetric complication is listed for HELLP syndrome?
questions.exp: Placental abruption is a listed HELLP complication. (Book p407)

questions.q: Which set contains other HELLP complications in the source notes?
opts: Pulmonary edema, DIC, and rupture of liver hematoma
questions.exp: Pulmonary edema, DIC, and rupture of liver hematoma are listed complications. (Book p407)

questions.q: Which classification is listed for HELLP syndrome?
questions.exp: HELLP is classified by the Mississippi classification. (Book p407)

questions.q: Which prior history is a risk factor for acute fatty liver of pregnancy?
questions.exp: Previous AFLP is a listed risk factor. (Book p407)

questions.q: Which pregnancy characteristics are listed as AFLP risk factors?
opts: Twin pregnancy and a male fetus
Singleton pregnancy with a female fetus only
questions.exp: Twin pregnancy and male fetus are listed AFLP risk factors. (Book p407)

questions.q: Which hypertensive disorder is a listed AFLP risk factor?
questions.exp: Pre-eclampsia is listed as an AFLP risk factor. (Book p407)

questions.q: What does LCHAD stand for in AFLP pathophysiology?
questions.exp: LCHAD is long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl coenzyme A dehydrogenase. (Book p407)

questions.q: What metabolic process requires LCHAD?
questions.exp: LCHAD is required for long-chain fatty-acid metabolism. (Book p407)

questions.q: Which fetal/maternal enzyme-status combination is linked to AFLP?
opts: Fetal homozygous LCHAD deficiency with maternal heterozygous deficiency
Maternal homozygous LCHAD with fetal normal enzyme only
questions.exp: The pathway shows fetal homozygous LCHAD deficiency and maternal heterozygous deficiency. (Book p407)

questions.q: What occurs in the mother when fatty-acid intermediates enter her circulation and she has limited oxidative capacity?
opts: All bile acids are cleared rapidly from the maternal circulation
Fatty acid accumulates in the liver and free radicals form
Placental blood flow returns to normal once clearance starts
Fetal insulin secretion falls, improving the fetal condition
questions.exp: When fatty-acid intermediates enter the maternal circulation with limited oxidative capacity, fatty acid accumulates in the liver and free radicals form. (Book p407)

questions.q: Fill up: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is linked to fetal deficiency of ______, which causes the mother to accumulate ______.
opts: long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase; medium and long chain fatty acids
ornithine transcarbamylase; ammonia in the blood
questions.exp: A fatty acid oxidation defect in the fetus (often LCHAD deficiency) floods the maternal liver with fatty acids, producing microvesicular steatosis. (Book p407)

questions.q: Which organ failures are directly shown in the AFLP pathway?
questions.exp: The pathway shows liver failure and renal failure, with raised urea/creatinine. (Book p407)

questions.q: Which metabolic complications are shown in AFLP liver failure?
opts: Hypoglycemia, raised ammonia, and risk of DIC
questions.exp: Liver failure in AFLP is associated with hypoglycemia, ↑NH3, and DIC risk. (Book p407)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about acute fatty liver of pregnancy is TRUE?
opts: Hypoglycaemia, a prolonged prothrombin time and encephalopathy with only modest transaminase rise are typical
A transaminase above 1000 IU/L with normal glucose rules the diagnosis out
Third-trimester jaundice with ascites and hypoalbuminaemia is always HELLP syndrome
Acute fatty liver is a first-trimester disorder that complicates hyperemesis gravidarum
questions.exp: AFLP gives liver failure with hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy but only moderate transaminase rise, unlike the high transaminases of viral hepatitis. (Book p407)

questions.q: What is the most common cause of liver failure in females according to the notes?
questions.exp: AFLP is listed as the most common cause of liver failure in females. (Book p408)

questions.q: At what gestational interval is AFLP commonly present?
questions.exp: AFLP commonly presents in the third trimester around 30–36 weeks. (Book p408)

questions.q: What are the most common symptoms at presentation of AFLP?
questions.exp: Nausea and vomiting are the most common presentation symptoms. (Book p408)

questions.q: Which set reflects fulminant liver failure features of AFLP?
opts: Jaundice, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and DIC
questions.exp: Fulminant liver failure in AFLP can cause jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy, and DIC. (Book p408)

questions.q: What diagnostic criteria are used for AFLP?
questions.exp: AFLP is diagnosed using Swansea criteria. (Book p408)

questions.q: Which finding favors AFLP over HELLP syndrome?
opts: Hyperammonaemia with mental confusion and hypoglycaemia
Hypertension alone, with no other metabolic disturbance
The degree of proteinuria, which is heavier in HELLP
A normal blood glucose level with preserved liver function
questions.exp: Hyperammonaemia with mental confusion and hypoglycaemia favour AFLP over HELLP syndrome. (Book p408)

questions.q: What glucose value is a differentiating AFLP feature in the notes?
questions.exp: Hypoglycemia below 72 mg/dL favors AFLP. (Book p408)

questions.q: Which coagulation pattern is a differentiating AFLP feature?
opts: DIC with increased PT, aPTT, and FDP plus reduced fibrinogen
Shortened PT and raised fibrinogen only
questions.exp: AFLP differentiation includes DIC with ↑PT/aPTT/FDP and ↓fibrinogen. (Book p408)

questions.q: Which associated complications favor AFLP over HELLP?
opts: Only a ventricular septal defect, which is commoner with HELLP syndrome
Only thyroid storm, which complicates severe pre-eclampsia
Only hypertension, which is the hallmark of AFLP rather than HELLP
Pancreatitis, transient diabetes insipidus and renal failure
questions.exp: Pancreatitis, transient diabetes insipidus and renal failure point to acute fatty liver; hypertension and proteinuria point to HELLP. (Book p408)

questions.q: What is the management sequence for AFLP?
opts: Maternal stabilization followed by prompt delivery
Wait for liver tests to normalize before delivery
questions.exp: AFLP requires maternal stabilization then prompt delivery. (Book p408)

questions.q: How soon does liver function return to normal after delivery in AFLP according to the notes?
questions.exp: Liver function returns to normal within 1 week after delivery. (Book p408)

questions.q: All of the following favour acute fatty liver of pregnancy over HELLP syndrome EXCEPT:
opts: Marked prolongation of the prothrombin time and hypofibrinogenaemia
Deep jaundice progressing to hepatic encephalopathy
questions.exp: Hypertension and proteinuria are the hallmarks of pre-eclampsia and HELLP; hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy and encephalopathy point to AFLP. (Book p408)

questions.q: In what patient and trimester is intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy typically seen?
opts: A genetically predisposed woman in the third trimester
Any man in the first trimester
questions.exp: ICP is seen in genetically predisposed females in the third trimester. (Book p408)

questions.q: Which hormonal pattern predisposes to ICP according to the notes?
questions.exp: Genetic susceptibility plus increased estrogen and progesterone predispose to ICP. (Book p408)

questions.q: What is the core pathophysiologic change in ICP?
opts: Incomplete bile-acid clearance causing plasma accumulation
questions.exp: Bile acids are incompletely cleared and accumulate in plasma. (Book p408)

questions.q: Which description of ICP is correct?
opts: Unique to pregnancy, high risk, reversible, and recurrent
A permanent disorder that never recurs
A condition only after molar pregnancy
questions.exp: ICP is a pregnancy-specific high-risk condition that is reversible and recurrent. (Book p408)

questions.q: What is the first symptom of ICP?
questions.exp: Pruritus is the first symptom of ICP. (Book p408)

questions.q: Where and when is ICP pruritus characteristically most marked?
opts: Palms and soles, most commonly at night
questions.exp: ICP pruritus has a predilection for palms/soles and is most common at night. (Book p408)

questions.q: How long before jaundice does pruritus typically occur in ICP?
opts: At exactly the same moment only
questions.exp: Pruritus precedes jaundice by about 4 weeks. (Book p408)

questions.q: Fill up: The itch of intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is worst on the ______ and usually begins in the ______ trimester.
questions.exp: Palmoplantar pruritus without a rash, worse at night and appearing in the third trimester, is characteristic; jaundice follows in a minority. (Book p408)

questions.q: How can elevated bile acids contribute to postpartum and antepartum hemorrhage?
opts: They eliminate coagulation factors directly in all cases
questions.exp: Bile acids reduce vitamin K absorption, increasing PPH and APH risk. (Book p408)

questions.q: How can accumulated bile acids precipitate preterm labor?
opts: They cause cervical cerclage failure only
questions.exp: Bile acids irritate the uterus, leading to preterm labor and RDS risk. (Book p408)

questions.q: How do bile acids contribute to meconium aspiration syndrome in ICP?
opts: Bile acids act only on maternal skin and cause itching, with no fetal effect
Bile acids reduce amniotic fluid production to zero and arrest fetal gut motility
Swallowed bile-salt-rich fluid irritates the fetal bowel and triggers meconium passage
Bile acids paralyse fetal bowel activity so that no meconium is passed at all
questions.exp: Bile salts in the amniotic fluid are swallowed by the fetus, irritate the bowel and trigger meconium passage, which underlies meconium-stained liquor and aspiration syndrome in ICP. (Book p409)

questions.q: What lethal fetal sequence is described when bile acids accumulate in the fetal heart?
questions.exp: Bile acids can accumulate in the fetal heart, causing cardiac arrest and stillbirth. (Book p409)

questions.q: What is the first/best investigation for ICP?
questions.exp: Serum bile acids are the first and best investigation. (Book p409)

questions.q: What serum bile-acid level supports ICP diagnosis in the notes?
questions.exp: A serum bile-acid level above 10 micromoles/L supports ICP. (Book p409)

questions.q: Which liver-test pattern may be seen in ICP?
opts: SGOT/SGPT less than twice normal and bilirubin below 5 mg/dL
AST/ALT more than ten times normal only
questions.exp: The notes give raised SGOT/SGPT less than twice normal and bilirubin less than 5 mg/dL. (Book p409)

questions.q: Match the finding with its role in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy — 1) Raised serum bile acids 2) Modestly raised transaminases 3) Pruritus without a primary rash … A) The most sensitive and diagnostic abnormality B) A supportive feature, usually only two to three times normal C) The presenting symptom, characteristically worse at night
questions.exp: Bile acids above 10 micromol/L are diagnostic, transaminases are supportive, and there is no primary rash — only excoriations from scratching. (Book p409)

questions.q: What maternal medication regimen is listed for ICP?
opts: Ursodeoxycholic acid plus vitamin K injection
questions.exp: ICP maternal treatment is ursodeoxycholic acid with vitamin K injection. (Book p409)

questions.q: When does intrapartum fetal monitoring begin for ICP?
questions.exp: Intrapartum fetal monitoring begins at 32 weeks. (Book p409)

questions.q: What is the stated surveillance schedule in ICP?
opts: No biophysical profile at all, since bile acid levels alone guide management
Weekly non-stress test and biophysical profile, with growth scans every three weeks
Daily ultrasound examination of the fetus and the placenta alone
A monthly non-stress test until the planned delivery
questions.exp: Surveillance in cholestasis is intensified because of the stillbirth risk: weekly testing with growth scans every three weeks. (Book p409)

questions.q: When is termination/induction planned for ICP?
questions.exp: Induction is planned at 36–37 weeks. (Book p409)

questions.q: What prophylaxis is listed for the newborn after an ICP pregnancy?
questions.exp: The notes specify vitamin K injection to the newborn. (Book p409)

questions.q: Which medication is contraindicated in the ICP note?
questions.exp: OCPs are contraindicated in the ICP note, which also notes increased gallstone risk. (Book p409)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is TRUE?
opts: Ursodeoxycholic acid relieves the itch and improves biochemistry, and delivery is offered from 37-38 weeks because of stillbirth risk
Antihistamines cure the condition, so pregnancy may safely continue to 42 weeks
Warfarin is the anticoagulant of choice when vitamin K deficiency causes a prolonged prothrombin time
A widespread urticarial rash always precedes the pruritus of intrahepatic cholestasis
questions.exp: Ursodeoxycholic acid is first-line; vitamin K is given to the mother to prevent haemorrhage and warfarin is unsafe in pregnancy. (Book p409)

questions.q: Where is the Rh antigen locus located according to the notes?
questions.exp: The Rh antigen locus is on the short arm of chromosome 1. (Book p410)

questions.q: Which set lists the Rh antigens given in the source?
opts: C, c, D, E, and e
questions.exp: The listed Rh antigens are C, c, D, E, and e. (Book p410)

questions.q: Around what gestational age does Rh antigen formation occur according to the notes?
questions.exp: Rh antigen formation is stated to occur by 38 days of gestation. (Book p410)

questions.q: What maternal-fetal pairing defines an Rh-negative pregnancy at risk?
questions.exp: An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus is the high-risk pairing. (Book p410)

questions.q: What paternal result makes the fetus definitively Rh-negative and removes the Rh-related high-risk concern in the source flowchart?
questions.exp: If the father is Rh-negative, the fetus will be Rh-negative and is not high risk in the source diagram. (Book p410)

questions.q: What fetal Rh-positive probability is shown when the father is Rh-positive in the source flowchart?
questions.exp: The source diagram gives a 50% chance of an Rh-positive fetus when the father is Rh-positive. (Book p410)

questions.q: Fill up: The clinically most important Rh antibody is ______, and without prophylaxis about ______ of Rh-negative women carrying an Rh-positive fetus become sensitised.
questions.exp: Anti-D is the antibody that matters; roughly 15% of at-risk women are immunised by a pregnancy or delivery unless anti-D immunoglobulin is given. (Book p410)

questions.q: What testing should be done at the first antenatal visit before identifying an Rh-negative mother?
questions.exp: ABO and Rh typing are done at the first ANC visit. (Book p411)

questions.q: What paternal assessment is required after identifying an Rh-negative pregnant woman?
opts: No paternal assessment is ever relevant
questions.exp: The husband's Rh type must be assessed in an Rh-negative pregnancy. (Book p411)

questions.q: Which events are listed as causes of fetomaternal hemorrhage in an Rh-negative mother?
questions.exp: Bleeding, invasive procedures, and versions are listed causes of fetomaternal hemorrhage. (Book p411)

questions.q: What is the first antibody produced when an Rh-negative mother is exposed to Rh antigen?
questions.exp: IgM is produced initially after Rh antigen exposure. (Book p411)

questions.q: Why is the first Rh-positive pregnancy generally safe in an unsensitized Rh-negative mother?
opts: All Rh-positive fetuses are Rh-negative in first pregnancy
Initially produced IgM cannot cross the placenta; IgG is produced after delivery
Maternal IgG cannot ever be made
Fetal red cells cannot enter maternal blood
questions.exp: The initial antibody is IgM, which cannot cross the placenta; significant IgG follows after delivery. (Book p411)

questions.q: Why is a subsequent Rh-positive pregnancy at risk after previous sensitization?
opts: IgG is formed quickly and crosses the placenta to hemolyze fetal cells
questions.exp: Prior exposure prompts rapid IgG formation; IgG crosses the placenta and causes fetal hemolysis. (Book p411)

questions.q: Match the manifestation with its mechanism — 1) Hydrops fetalis 2) Kernicterus 3) Early neonatal anaemia … A) Unconjugated bilirubin deposition in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei B) Severe anaemia with ascites, scalp oedema and an enlarged placenta C) Ongoing haemolysis in the first days of life needing phototherapy or exchange transfusion
questions.exp: Severe haemolysis causes hydrops in utero, bilirubin causes kernicterus after birth, and continuing antibody action causes early neonatal anaemia. (Book p411)

questions.q: What is the initiating fetal complication of Rh isoimmunization?
questions.exp: Rh antibodies cause fetal hemolysis. (Book p412)

questions.q: What severe sequence can follow fetal anemia in Rh isoimmunization?
opts: Heart failure followed by hydrops fetalis
questions.exp: Severe fetal anemia causes heart failure and then hydrops fetalis. (Book p412)

questions.q: What compensatory response produces erythroblastosis fetalis?
opts: Hepatosplenomegaly and bone-marrow hyperplasia increasing erythrocytes
Reduced erythropoiesis within the fetal bone marrow and liver
Fetal insulin suppression from maternal antibody transfer
Maternal platelet activation with consumptive coagulopathy
questions.exp: Erythroblastosis fetalis reflects the compensatory response of hepatosplenomegaly and bone-marrow hyperplasia producing more erythrocytes. (Book p412)

questions.q: Which maternal complications are linked to placentomegaly in Rh disease?
questions.exp: Placentomegaly can cause PIH and polyhydramnios. (Book p412)

questions.q: What CTG/NST pattern can indicate fetal anemia?
questions.exp: A sinusoidal heart-wave pattern on CTG/NST is an indication of fetal anemia. (Book p412)

questions.q: What MCA Doppler value indicates fetal anemia?
opts: Peak systolic velocity less than 0.5 MoM
Peak systolic velocity at least 1.5 MoM
questions.exp: MCA peak systolic velocity ≥1.5 MoM signals fetal anemia. (Book p412)

questions.q: Which is a listed cause of fetal anemia besides Rh isoimmunization?
opts: Vasa previa or twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
questions.exp: The notes list Rh isoimmunization, vasa previa, and twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome as causes. (Book p412)

questions.q: Fill up: Fetal anaemia is detected non-invasively by Doppler of the ______, where a peak systolic velocity above ______ multiples of the median suggests severe anaemia.
questions.exp: Anaemia lowers blood viscosity and raises middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity; above 1.5 multiples of the median it predicts severe anaemia. (Book p412)

questions.q: What is anti-D?
opts: An antigen that sensitizes the mother
questions.exp: Anti-D is an antibody against the Rh antigen. (Book p412)

questions.q: How does externally administered anti-D prevent Rh sensitization?
opts: It increases fetal haemolysis, clearing Rh-positive cells from the circulation
It converts the fetal Rh type from positive to negative while in utero
It neutralises Rh-positive fetal red cells before maternal antibodies form
It stimulates the mother to produce her own protective anti-D antibodies
questions.exp: Externally administered anti-D neutralises Rh-positive fetal red cells before the maternal immune system mounts stimulation and forms excess antibodies. (Book p412)

questions.q: In which pregnancy is anti-D beneficial?
opts: An Rh-positive mother with no antibody screen
Any pregnancy regardless of Rh type
questions.exp: Anti-D is beneficial only in Rh-negative unsensitized pregnancies. (Book p412)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about anti-D immunoglobulin is TRUE?
opts: Anti-D clears Rh-positive fetal red cells from the maternal circulation before the mother can mount her own immune response
Anti-D is a live vaccine that must be given before pregnancy to work
Anti-D given after delivery protects the infant by suppressing the fetal immune system
Anti-D is effective only in the first trimester and is never given after delivery
questions.exp: Passive anti-D causes rapid clearance of fetal cells so the mother never makes her own antibody; it is given after any sensitising event and at 28 weeks. (Book p412)

questions.q: What low anti-D dose is listed for routine prophylaxis?
questions.exp: The routine low dose is 300 micrograms of anti-D. (Book p413)

questions.q: A 300-microgram anti-D dose neutralizes up to what volume of fetomaternal hemorrhage?
questions.exp: Three hundred micrograms neutralizes up to 30 mL of fetomaternal hemorrhage. (Book p413)

questions.q: A 300-microgram anti-D dose neutralizes up to what volume of fetal red cells?
questions.exp: The stated coverage is 15 mL of fetal RBCs. (Book p413)

questions.q: What is the stated effect if prophylactic anti-D crosses the placenta?
opts: It does not cause fetal hemolysis
questions.exp: The notes state that anti-D does not cause hemolysis even if it crosses the placenta. (Book p413)

questions.q: What is the purpose of the indirect Coombs test in an Rh-negative pregnant woman?
opts: To determine whether she is sensitized
questions.exp: ICT assesses whether an Rh-negative pregnant woman is sensitized. (Book p413)

questions.q: What sample is used for indirect Coombs testing?
questions.exp: ICT is performed on maternal blood. (Book p413)

questions.q: When is ICT performed in Rh-negative pregnancy?
opts: At the first ANC visit and repeated at 28 weeks
questions.exp: ICT is done at booking and repeated at 28 weeks. (Book p413)

questions.q: What does a negative ICT indicate in the Rh-negative management pathway?
questions.exp: Negative ICT indicates that the Rh-negative mother is unsensitized. (Book p413)

questions.q: What does a positive ICT indicate in the Rh-negative management pathway?
questions.exp: Positive ICT indicates Rh sensitization. (Book p413)

questions.q: What antepartum prophylaxis is given to an unsensitized Rh-negative woman whose ICT remains negative?
questions.exp: A negative ICT receives 300 micrograms or 1,500 IU anti-D antepartum. (Book p413)

questions.q: What is the role of anti-D after ICT is positive?
opts: Stop all fetal monitoring, since sensitisation is inevitable
No role; manage as a sensitized Rh-negative pregnancy
Give double the routine dose of anti-D immediately
Give anti-D every day until delivery is achieved
questions.exp: Once the indirect Coombs test is positive, anti-D has no role and the pregnancy is managed as a sensitized Rh-negative pregnancy. (Book p413)

questions.q: Fill up: The indirect Coombs test detects ______ in the mother's serum, whereas the direct Coombs test detects ______.
opts: free anti-D antibody; antibody already bound to fetal red cells
fetal red cells in maternal blood; free anti-D antibody
maternal red cell antigens; maternal anti-D antibody
questions.exp: Indirect Coombs screens maternal serum for free antibody; direct Coombs shows antibody already coating the infant's red cells and is positive in affected babies. (Book p413)

questions.q: What delivery timing is listed for an unsensitized Rh-negative woman?
questions.exp: For unsensitized Rh-negative women, delivery is at 39–40 weeks. (Book p413)

questions.q: What delivery mode is listed for an unsensitized Rh-negative woman?
questions.exp: Vaginal delivery is the listed mode. (Book p413)

questions.q: What cord-clamping practice is stated to prevent sensitization during delivery of an unsensitized Rh-negative mother?
questions.exp: Early cord clamping is listed to prevent sensitization during delivery in an unsensitized mother. (Book p413)

questions.q: After delivery of an Rh-positive newborn, which test is performed on the newborn blood?
opts: Indirect Coombs test on maternal blood only
questions.exp: A Rh-positive newborn has direct Coombs test (DCT) on newborn blood. (Book p413)

questions.q: When is 300 micrograms of postpartum anti-D given to the mother after an Rh-positive newborn?
opts: If the newborn DCT is negative
questions.exp: A Rh-positive newborn with negative DCT leads to 300 micrograms anti-D to the mother. (Book p413)

questions.q: Is postpartum anti-D prophylaxis required if the newborn is Rh-negative?
opts: Only if maternal blood group is A
questions.exp: If the newborn is Rh-negative, postpartum prophylaxis is not required. (Book p413)

questions.q: What is the aim of postpartum anti-D prophylaxis?
questions.exp: Postpartum anti-D is intended to protect a future pregnancy. (Book p413)

questions.q: What is the ideal time for postpartum anti-D after vaginal delivery or cesarean?
questions.exp: Postpartum anti-D should ideally be given within 72 hours; the notes permit up to 28 days. (Book p413)

questions.q: Should anti-D still be administered if postpartum sterilization is planned?
opts: Only if the baby is Rh-negative
questions.exp: The notes state anti-D is given even if postpartum sterilization is to be done. (Book p413)

questions.q: An Rh-negative woman with a negative antibody screen delivers an Rh-positive infant. The cord direct Coombs test is negative and the baby is well. What should she receive?
opts: Anti-D immunoglobulin 300 microgram (1500 IU) intramuscularly within 72 hours of delivery
Anti-D only if the Kleihauer-Betke test shows a bleed larger than 30 mL
Nothing, because the baby is unaffected and her antibody screen is negative
Anti-D 50 microgram now and a further dose at her six-week postnatal visit
questions.exp: All non-sensitised Rh-negative women delivering an Rh-positive infant need anti-D within 72 hours; the Kleihauer-Betke test only decides whether extra doses are needed. (Book p413)

questions.q: Why is maternal antibody titre measured in sensitized Rh-negative pregnancy?
opts: To measure the maternal blood glucose concentration during treatment
To confirm the diagnosis of pregnancy-induced hypertension
To judge whether the antibody level is high enough to cross the placenta and cause haemolysis
To determine the sex of the fetus before planning delivery
questions.exp: A critical titre means there is enough antibody crossing the placenta to produce significant fetal haemolysis, and it triggers surveillance. (Book p414)

questions.q: What is the critical maternal antibody titre in the source notes?
questions.exp: The critical titre is 1:16; serially diluted maternal antibody at or above this is significant. (Book p414)

questions.q: Which titre is considered not significant in the management flowchart?
questions.exp: Titre below 1:16 is not significant. (Book p414)

questions.q: How frequently is antibody titre repeated when it is below the critical level?
questions.exp: With titre below 1:16, repeat titres every 4 weeks. (Book p414)

questions.q: When does fetal monitoring begin for antibody titre below the critical threshold?
questions.exp: Fetal monitoring begins from 32 weeks in this pathway. (Book p414)

questions.q: When is delivery planned if the antibody titre remains below 1:16?
questions.exp: With non-significant titre, delivery is at 37–38 weeks. (Book p414)

questions.q: What is the best noninvasive investigation for fetal anemia?
questions.exp: MCA Doppler is the best noninvasive investigation and screening test for fetal anemia. (Book p414)

questions.q: At what MCA peak systolic velocity is fetal anemia considered positive?
questions.exp: MCA PSV ≥1.5 MoM indicates fetal anemia. (Book p414)

questions.q: When MCA PSV is below 1.5 MoM in a sensitized pregnancy, how often should it be repeated?
questions.exp: If MCA PSV is <1.5 MoM, repeat it every 1–2 weeks. (Book p414)

questions.q: What antenatal fetal surveillance is used from 32 weeks when MCA PSV remains below 1.5 MoM?
questions.exp: The pathway calls for weekly NST and BPP from 32 weeks. (Book p414)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about Rh isoimmunisation is TRUE?
opts: Sensitisation during one pregnancy usually spares that baby but endangers later Rh-positive pregnancies
A first Rh-positive pregnancy is always severely affected because antibodies form in the first trimester
Anti-D immunoglobulin given after sensitisation reverses the immune response
ABO incompatibility between mother and fetus makes Rh sensitisation more likely
questions.exp: Primary immunisation is slow, so the index pregnancy usually escapes; ABO incompatibility protects, because fetal cells are destroyed before they immunise. (Book p414)

questions.q: What is the next diagnostic procedure if MCA PSV is 1.5 MoM or greater?
opts: Cordocentesis to assess fetal Hb and hematocrit
questions.exp: MCA PSV ≥1.5 MoM indicates anemia and prompts cordocentesis for fetal Hb/hematocrit. (Book p414)

questions.q: Cordocentesis samples blood from where?
questions.exp: Cordocentesis obtains blood from the umbilical cord. (Book p415)

questions.q: Which cordocentesis finding is classified as mild fetal anemia?
opts: Fetal Hb less than 2 SD below mean or hematocrit below 30%
Fetal Hb more than 2 SD below mean only
questions.exp: Mild anemia is Hb <2 SD below mean or Hct <30% in the source flowchart. (Book p415)

questions.q: Which cordocentesis finding is classified as severe fetal anemia?
opts: Fetal Hb more than 2 SD below mean or hematocrit below 30%
Hb less than 2 SD below mean only
questions.exp: Severe anemia is Hb >2 SD below mean (i.e., deviation) or hematocrit <30% in the source diagram. (Book p415)

questions.q: How are fetal Hb and hematocrit followed in mild fetal anemia?
questions.exp: For mild anemia, repeat fetal Hb and hematocrit weekly. (Book p415)

questions.q: When is delivery planned for mild fetal anemia after surveillance?
questions.exp: Mild fetal anemia is delivered at 37–38 weeks. (Book p415)

questions.q: What is the management for severe fetal anemia at 35 weeks or later?
questions.exp: Severe fetal anemia at ≥35 weeks is managed by delivery. (Book p415)

questions.q: What is the management for severe fetal anemia before 35 weeks?
questions.exp: Severe anemia before 35 weeks is managed with intrauterine blood transfusion. (Book p415)

questions.q: What cord-clamping practice is used when an Rh-negative mother is already sensitized (ICT positive)?
questions.exp: Because the mother is already sensitized, the source lists delayed cord clamping. (Book p415)

questions.q: A sensitised woman with anti-D antibodies at 32 weeks has a middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity of 1.7 multiples of the median. What is the next step?
opts: Cordocentesis with intrauterine transfusion if the fetal haemoglobin is low, after corticosteroids for lung maturity
Immediate delivery at 32 weeks without further testing
Repeat the middle cerebral artery Doppler in four weeks
Maternal intravenous immunoglobulin and expectant management to term
questions.exp: A peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median indicates severe anaemia, confirmed by cordocentesis and treated by intrauterine transfusion. (Book p415)

questions.q: What volume of fetomaternal hemorrhage is considered normal in the source notes?
questions.exp: Normal FMH is less than 4 mL. (Book p415)

questions.q: How much additional anti-D is given for every extra 1 mL of fetal blood above 30 mL FMH?
questions.exp: For each extra 1 mL fetal blood over 30 mL, add 10 micrograms anti-D. (Book p415)

questions.q: Which event is a listed cause of increased fetomaternal hemorrhage?
questions.exp: Abdominal trauma is among causes of increased FMH. (Book p415)

questions.q: Which delivery/procedure event is a listed cause of increased fetomaternal hemorrhage?
opts: An early fetal echocardiogram performed before 20 weeks
A DIPSI glucose tolerance test in the second trimester
A routine fundal examination at the antenatal visit
Instrumental delivery or manual removal of the placenta
questions.exp: Delivery itself, especially instrumental delivery and manual removal of the placenta, is the commonest cause of a larger feto-maternal haemorrhage. (Book p415)

questions.q: Which pregnancy events are listed as causes of increased fetomaternal hemorrhage?
questions.exp: Twin pregnancy and intrauterine death are listed causes of increased FMH. (Book p415)

questions.q: Match the test with what it does — 1) Kleihauer-Betke test 2) Rosette test 3) Flow cytometry … A) A screening test that detects a feto-maternal haemorrhage of more than about 10 mL B) A quantitative test that uses acid elution of adult haemoglobin to identify fetal cells C) The most accurate modern method of quantifying fetal red cells in maternal blood
questions.exp: The rosette test screens, Kleihauer-Betke quantifies by acid elution, and flow cytometry with anti-HbF is the most precise method. (Book p415)

questions.q: What is the screening test for increased fetomaternal hemorrhage?
questions.exp: Rosette test is the screening test for increased FMH. (Book p416)

questions.q: What does a positive rosette test indicate?
questions.exp: A positive rosette test indicates increased FMH. (Book p416)

questions.q: Which test quantitatively estimates the exact volume of fetomaternal hemorrhage?
questions.exp: Kleihauer–Betke is the quantitative test for exact FMH volume. (Book p416)

questions.q: Within what interval should the Kleihauer–Betke test be done according to the notes?
questions.exp: The source states the Kleihauer–Betke test should be done within 2 hours. (Book p416)

questions.q: What type of test is the Singer alkali denaturation test?
opts: Quantitative test of exact FMH volume
questions.exp: Singer alkali denaturation is a qualitative test. (Book p416)

questions.q: What bleeding differential can Singer alkali denaturation test distinguish?
questions.exp: Singer alkali test differentiates vasa previa and placenta previa and also helps detect FMH. (Book p416)

questions.q: Which first-trimester event is an indication for anti-D prophylaxis?
opts: Routine fetal movement counting from 28 weeks of gestation onwards
Normal glycosuria detected on routine antenatal urine testing
Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy or chorionic-villus sampling
Normal nausea and vomiting limited to the first trimester alone
questions.exp: First-trimester indications for anti-D prophylaxis include abortion, ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy and chorionic-villus sampling. (Book p416)

questions.q: What anti-D dose is listed by ACOG/India for sensitizing events before 12 weeks?
opts: No anti-D is used before 12 weeks
questions.exp: For <12 weeks, the source follows ACOG in India: 50 micrograms IM. (Book p416)

questions.q: What anti-D dose is listed by RCOG for sensitizing events before 12 weeks?
questions.exp: The RCOG dose listed for <12 weeks is 300 micrograms IM. (Book p416)

questions.q: Which second/third-trimester procedure is an indication for anti-D?
opts: A detailed fetal echocardiogram performed before 20 weeks
Amniocentesis, or external cephalic or internal podalic version
A DIPSI glucose tolerance test in the second trimester
A routine non-stress test in the third trimester
questions.exp: Anti-D is given after any procedure that may cause feto-maternal haemorrhage, including amniocentesis and version. (Book p416)

questions.q: Which second/third-trimester events are indications for anti-D prophylaxis?
opts: Unexplained bleeding, APH, fetal death, or abdominal trauma
questions.exp: The source lists unexplained bleeding, APH, fetal death, and abdominal trauma. (Book p416)

questions.q: What anti-D dose is given after sensitizing events beyond 12 weeks?
questions.exp: The stated dose after 12 weeks is 300 micrograms IM. (Book p416)

questions.q: Fill up: A single 300 microgram dose of anti-D covers about ______ mL of fetal whole blood, so a 40 mL feto-maternal haemorrhage needs ______ doses.
questions.exp: 300 microgram neutralises about 30 mL of fetal blood; the Kleihauer-Betke result is used to calculate any additional doses required. (Book p416)

questions.q: Why is there no role for anti-D with cordocentesis?
opts: The mother is already sensitized (ICT positive)
The procedure has no fetal blood exposure
questions.exp: The notes say no anti-D with cordocentesis because sensitization has already occurred. (Book p416)

questions.q: Why is anti-D not required if delivery occurs within 28 days of a prior anti-D dose?
opts: The half-life of anti-D is 28 days
Anti-D cannot cross placenta after 28 days
questions.exp: The source states anti-D half-life is 28 days, so no repeat is needed for delivery within that interval. (Book p416)

questions.q: Which minor antigen carries the most common risk of sensitization?
questions.exp: Kell is listed as the most common minor antigen leading to sensitization, often after mismatched transfusion. (Book p416)

questions.q: Which minor antigens are listed as carrying sensitization risk?
questions.exp: Kell, Kidd, and Duffy-A are in the risk-of-sensitization group. (Book p416)

questions.q: Which minor antigens are listed as not carrying sensitization risk?
questions.exp: Lewis, I antigen, and Duffy-B are listed as no-risk minor antigens. (Book p416)

questions.q: All of the following are indications for anti-D immunoglobulin EXCEPT:
opts: A woman who is herself Rh-positive
Delivery of an Rh-positive infant by an Rh-negative mother
Antepartum haemorrhage in an Rh-negative woman
External cephalic version in an Rh-negative woman
questions.exp: Anti-D is only for Rh-negative non-sensitised women exposed to Rh-positive blood; Rh-positive women cannot form anti-D. (Book p416)

questions.q: What is the most common non-D alloimmunization according to the notes?
questions.exp: Anti-E is listed as the most common non-D alloimmunization. (Book p417)

questions.q: What is the most severe non-D alloimmunization according to the notes?
questions.exp: Anti-C is listed as the most severe non-D alloimmunization. (Book p417)

questions.q: What is mirror/Ballantyne syndrome?
opts: Only maternal edema without fetal findings
Mother and fetus mimic each other with edema
Only fetal edema with a normal mother
questions.exp: Mirror syndrome means the mother and fetus mirror each other; both are edematous. (Book p417)

questions.q: Which pairing describes the mother and fetus in mirror syndrome?
opts: Maternal oligohydramnios and fetal IUGR only
Maternal hyperglycemia and fetal hypoglycemia only
Maternal anemia and fetal polycythemia only
questions.exp: In mirror syndrome, maternal polyhydramnios accompanies fetal hydrops. (Book p417)

questions.q: Which condition is associated with mirror syndrome?
opts: Anti-D isoimmunisation, twin-to-twin transfusion, cystic hygroma or placental chorioangioma
An uncomplicated singleton pregnancy with a normal fetus and placenta
Diet-controlled gestational diabetes with a normal liquor volume
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy alone, with raised serum bile acids
questions.exp: Mirror syndrome is the maternal reflection of fetal hydrops, whatever its cause — immune, anastomotic, lymphatic or placental. (Book p417)

questions.q: How is hydrops fetalis diagnosed by ultrasound?
opts: Fetal anemia alone without ultrasound findings
At least two of pericardial effusion, ascites, pleural effusion, and subcutaneous edema
questions.exp: Hydrops is diagnosed if at least two of the four listed fluid/edema findings are present. (Book p417)

questions.q: What is the first ultrasound sign of hydrops fetalis in the notes?
opts: Buddha sign from scalp subcutaneous edema
questions.exp: The first USG sign is Buddha sign due to scalp subcutaneous edema. (Book p417)

questions.q: Are placentomegaly and polyhydramnios diagnostic criteria for hydrops fetalis?
opts: Yes; either one alone diagnoses hydrops
No; they are associated findings only
questions.exp: Placentomegaly and polyhydramnios are findings in hydrops, not diagnostic criteria. (Book p417)

questions.q: What is the most common cause/type context of immune hydrops fetalis in the notes?
questions.exp: Immune hydrops is listed in Rh-negative pregnancy. (Book p417)

questions.q: What fetal Hb and hematocrit thresholds are shown for immune hydrops?
questions.exp: The immune-hydrops box lists fetal Hb <40% and hematocrit <15%. (Book p417)

questions.q: What is the most common cause of nonimmune hydrops fetalis?
questions.exp: Nonimmune hydrops is more common; CVS anomaly is its most common listed cause. (Book p417)

questions.q: Which categories are listed as other causes of nonimmune hydrops?
opts: Rh D isoimmunisation alone, which is the only listed cause
Maternal obesity alone, acting through an unexplained mechanism
Maternal hyperthyroidism alone, causing fetal tachycardia
Chromosomal anomalies, parvovirus B19 or TORCH infection, and fetal anaemia
questions.exp: Non-immune hydrops has chromosomal, infective, haematological and cardiac causes; Rh disease is the immune category. (Book p417)

questions.q: Match the condition with its description — 1) Mirror syndrome 2) Immune hydrops 3) Non-immune hydrops … A) Maternal oedema, hypertension and proteinuria that parallel fetal hydrops and resolve after delivery B) Caused by red cell alloimmunisation, classically anti-D, anti-c or anti-Kell C) Caused by cardiac anomalies, arrhythmia, parvovirus B19 or twin-to-twin transfusion
questions.exp: Mirror syndrome is the maternal reflection of fetal hydrops; hydrops is now more often non-immune than immune in countries with anti-D prophylaxis. (Book p417)
